source.title: Rethinking Reflection in Pre-Training
source.authors: Darsh J. Shah; Peter Rushton; Somanshu Singla; Mohit Parmar; Kurt Smith; Yash Vanjani; A. Vaswani; Adarsh Chaluvaraju; Andrew Hojel; Andrew Ma; Anil Thomas; Anthony M. Polloreno; A. Tanwer; Burhan Drak Sibai; Divya S Mansingka; D. Shivaprasad; Ishaan Shah; K. Stratos; Khoi Nguyen; Michael Callahan; M. Pust; M. Iyer; Philip Monk; Platon Mazarakis; Ritvik Kapila; Saurabh Srivastava; T. Romanski

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether benchmark accuracy changes with training compute or model size, using adversarial reflection tasks rather than held-out pretraining loss or the original scaling-law method.
record.gate_note: The study reports benchmark accuracy correlations with log(pre-training compute) and qualitative Qwen2.5 accuracy trends, which bear on V6. Its reflection rates are not task performance, and its answer-conditioned perplexity comparison is not held-out pretraining loss; neither is recorded as a scaling-law result. It does not fit or test power laws, extrapolate losses, or find compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.test_reason: The study reports how accuracy on six adversarial reflection benchmarks changes with pre-training compute. It covers 40 OLMo-2 checkpoints (Pearson correlations with log compute) and six Qwen2.5 sizes. That is a new downstream setting bearing on V6. It fits no scaling curve, does not predict from loss, and has no loss-based results for V1–V5 or V7. T3 fits better than T2: the question is reflection, not scaling, and the scaling evidence is a by-product correlation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude reflection, both situational and self, appears early in pre-training and strengthens with more pre-training compute. Situational accuracy averages r≈0.76 with log compute. Self-reflection is rarer but advances. Better-pretrained models need less test-time compute.
record.recipe_differences: Measures adversarial reflection-task performance across pre-training checkpoints and model sizes, not held-out cross-entropy loss or fitted scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports different accuracy-compute correlations for situational-reflection versus self-reflection and across datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Explicit reflection rate rises with log compute (0.49–0.88), and the answer-conditioned perplexity gap narrows over pre-training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reflective behaviour, as distinct from task accuracy, emerges and grows with pre-training compute.

fits_no_version.finding: Test-time compute needed for fixed GSM8K-Platinum accuracy falls as train compute rises for OLMo-2-32B (Figure 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Train-time compute substitutes for test-time compute in reflection tasks.

record.problems: For this claim, the evidence is limited to benchmark accuracy correlations and qualitative plots; no scaling-law fit, loss-based prediction, or uncertainty estimate for the correlations is reported. The Qwen2.5 trend is given qualitatively in the text and graph.
record.rows_left_out: No individual Qwen2.5 task-by-size figure values were extracted because Figure 7 presents them graphically without tabulated values; the study's qualitative family-level result is recorded in r13. Reflection-rate metrics and conditional answer perplexity comparisons were excluded because they do not measure V6 task accuracy or held-out pretraining loss.

untested.parts: Prediction of downstream performance from pretraining loss; any fitted functional form or extrapolation of accuracy; conventional (non-adversarial) benchmarks.
All: no held-out pretraining loss vs N, D or C.

missing.what: No-trigger and 'Wait, I made a mistake' trigger accuracy on GSM8K-Platinum rising with pre-training compute

record.verdict_notes: The correlations pool checkpoints across three model sizes and give no uncertainty or fit, so they show monotone association, not 'predictability' in the scaling-law sense. Compute is estimated as 6ND. The paper cites Kaplan only in passing.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power laws fitted to smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their trends.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.

The study tests accuracy trends on adversarial reflection benchmarks against compute or model size, but not performance prediction from pretraining loss, fitted predictive curves, or generalization to conventional downstream tasks.
Dependence of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.

relationships.condition: OLMo-2 situational-reflection accuracy (six tasks) and self-reflection cruxeval-i
relationships.reason: Accuracy correlates 0.70–0.84 with log(pre-training compute) (r1–r6), and 0.69 for self-reflection cruxeval-i (r8).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy correlated 0.70–0.84 with log pretraining compute across six situational-reflection tasks and 0.69 on self-reflection cruxeval-i.

relationships.condition: OLMo-2 self-reflection accuracy on BBH, cruxeval-o, GSM8K, GSM8K-Platinum, TriviaQA
relationships.reason: Correlations are only 0.26–0.44 (r7, r9–r11) and 0.09 on TriviaQA (r12). The sets keep only items every checkpoint failed, which may suppress gains.
relationships.display_finding: Correlations were only 0.26–0.44 and 0.09 on TriviaQA, with evaluation restricted to items every checkpoint initially failed.

relationships.reason: The authors state performance consistently increases with parameter count (Figure 7). This is qualitative only (r13).
relationships.display_finding: Situational-reflection performance consistently increased with parameter size from 0.5B to 72B.
